newsitem.title: RWANDA: U.N. envoy says he narrows Rwanda, Zaire rift.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy says he narrows Rwanda, Zaire rift.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien said on Tuesday he had narrowed differences between Rwanda and Zaire and a summit between leaders of the countries was on the cards.

Chretien, special envoy of U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros Ghali, said he would leave for Kinshasa later on Tuesday for more talks with Zaire on a humanitarian force and the plight of more than a million Rwandan refugees trapped by fighting.
Zaire accuses Rwanda of backing rebels in eastern Zaire but Kigali says the Tutsi-inspired rebellion is the result of corrupt rule by Kinshasa and hatred of its out-of-control army.
"The whole idea of my mission is to narrow the wide differences between the two countries and bring them to a face- to-face meeting," Chretien, Canada's ambassador to the United States, told Reuters.
"I think I have managed to narrow the differences and we should have a (Rwanda-Zaire) meeting soon," he added.
On his second visit to Rwanda in days, Chretien said his talks with Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu and Vice-President and military strongman Major-General Paul Kagame were encouraging.

Chretien said he welcomed a Canadian offer to lead a multinational force to help end the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire, where many are feared dying from thirst and starvation. He said the force "will boost my peace mission".

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali confirmed on Tuesday that Canada was ready to command a multinational force for Zaire and said he hoped it would receive logistical support from the United States.
He said South Africa had agreed in principle to take part and he hoped in a few days to have a Security Council mandate.
France, Spain, Mali and Ethiopia have also pledged troops for a neutral international force approved by the U.N. Security Council to help end the humanitarian crisis in Zaire.
In a major climbdown, Kagame told reporters late on Monday Rwanda might agree to French participation in a U.N. force as long as Paris did not have a prominent role.
"We may agree so long as France does not get a prominent role. They can support the operation in many ways but keep out of major operational details," said the military chief.

Senior Rwandan military officials said a Canadian-led force would be welcome as Canada had no colonial history in Africa and combined the languages of French and English, a prerequisite for the Great Lakes region.
"Frankly they are about the best we can get because of language and lack of regional interests," an army officer said.

Rwanda had opposed French participation in the U.N. force as it considered Paris an ally of French-speaking Zaire and Rwanda's former Hutu-led government, which with its former army and a Hutu extremist militia largely controls the refugees.
France was the first to offer troops and said the force should be made up of 5,000 soldiers from numerous countries and stay no longer than two months.

European Commissioner Emma Bonino visited the northwestern Rwandan town of Gisenyi on Tuesday and officials said she and her delegation would try to cross into rebel-held eastern Zaire for an eyewitness assessement of the humanitarian crisis there.
